Pod in CrashLoopBackOff

A container keeps exiting and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with a growing delay. All playbooks.

5 steps

  1. See the restart count and the reason for the last exit. Look at Last State under each container, and at the events at the bottom.

    Describe a pod

    Shows a pod's status, container states, restart reasons and recent events.

    kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>

    pods, events, debugging

  2. Read the logs of the run that crashed, not the one that is starting now.

    Get logs from previously crashed pod

    Useful for checking why a pod crashed before it restarted.

    kubectl logs <pod-name> --previous

    logs, crash, debug

  3. If the reason is OOMKilled, compare the pod's memory with its limit, then raise the limit or fix the leak.

    PromQL: Pod memory usage

    Working-set memory per pod in MiB: the figure kubectl top shows and the kubelet uses for eviction.

    sum by (pod) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="<namespace>", container!=""}) / 1024 / 1024

    prometheus, promql, memory

  4. If the exit code is 1 or 2 straight after start, it is usually configuration: a missing environment variable, secret or config file. Check what the pod actually received.

    Get running pod YAML

    Exports the live YAML configuration of a running pod.

    kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o yaml

    yaml, export

  5. If the crashes began with a new release, roll back first and investigate after.

    Rollback a deployment

    Rolls back a deployment to the previous revision.

    kubectl rollout undo deployment/<deployment-name>

    rollback, undo, deployment
